Physics teacher here, what he is teaching is not physics. Physics is a mathematical description of nature. What he is teaching is a social studies class with a loose connection to the sciences. Not to say there is anything wrong with that, but it shouldn't be taught as a physics class. If these students go on to higher level physics courses they will not have the grounding in physical law and mathematics that they need to move forward.

Education Policy Student: I'm sure the students are still getting a great mathematical foundation in physics. There is a difference between changing standards and developing new curriculums. Although the teacher has altered his lesson plans to incorporate social justice themes, the physical principles that are taught are unchanged. I think its wonderful that a STEM teacher is taking an initiative to highlight the contributions of black scientists. Students need more of this!

If you read the links that another poster gave to the curriculum you will see that the homework assignments aren't physics. Going on a Google search to find a physicist for homework and solving one dimensional kinematics problems to help lay the foundation for two dimensional kinematics and force problems are just not the same thing. And physics is all math. If he wants to teach social studies instead of physics he should go back and get another degree and switch fields like everyone else that wants to teach a different subject. There he could ask these very same questions without putting his students at a disadvantage in the future by not teaching the standard physics curriculum. That's my view at least.

It's only a six-day curriculum. The students are not at a disadvantage because the yearly standards have not changed. One week of creative education will not set back students for the rest of their careers.

Maybe in other subjects you can get away with taking a whole week off, but not in physics. There is never enough time to cover every thing you need to cover in physics. I mean, I am trying to think about what would have to be cut to remove a whole 6 days from the class. Static Equilibrium? Conservation of Energy? Torque? I mean, there are other courses where you can take it easy and be loose with your topics, but not in physics or math. If you skip anything, the whole house of cards will come crashing down on the student later on (because everything builds on what came before). It's not like his idea is bad, but when you are teaching a class where the failure rate is already extremely high that is not the time or the place to be going off topic.

Why can't he stop teaching Physics if he wants to teach English/Lit so bad? Oh, because there's a shit ton of English teachers because it's easy and not a lot of Physics teachers because that takes effort. THERE'S your problem, teach!
